The modified convolution function reduces the mean absolute error for formation‑energy prediction from 0.112 eV/atom to 0.039 eV/atom, achieving DFT‑level accuracy comparable to the experimental DFT‑experiment error of 0.081–0.136 eV/atom.
CGCNN classifies metals versus semiconductors with an area under the ROC curve of 0.95 and an overall accuracy of 0.90.

By extracting per‑atom site energies in perovskites, the model reveals that large‑radius elements stabilize the A site and group 4‑6 elements stabilize the B site, and using these insights the high‑throughput search space for stable perovskites is reduced by a factor of seven (from 18,928 to 228 candidates).

When applied to a set of 1,585 crystals with elastic properties, CGCNN predicts bulk modulus with a mean absolute error of 0.077 log(GPa) and shear modulus with a mean absolute error of 0.114 log(GPa), demonstrating good generalization.
The Materials Project provides an open RESTful API and a high‑level Python library (pymatgen) that enable programmatic querying and analysis of the full dataset.

The workflow software FireWorks together with the custodian job‑management tool automatically manages high‑throughput DFT calculations, self‑heals failed runs, and applies material‑type‑specific workflows.

Visual warnings are displayed on the Materials Project website for compounds whose calculated oxidation states, cell volumes, or bond lengths deviate significantly from experimental norms, helping users assess data reliability.
Automated validation checks compare calculated oxidation states, cell volumes, and bond lengths against experimental data and flag outliers for user review.

Using Materials Project tools, researchers designed a new class of sodium‑based carbonophosphate compounds, predicted them to be thermodynamically stable, synthesized them hydrothermally, and experimentally confirmed their Li‑ion battery performance after ion exchange.

The Materials Project aims to reduce the typical 10–20 year timeline for advanced material development by providing large‑scale accurate information, thereby accelerating discovery for clean energy, electronics, and other sectors.

The distribution of chromium coordination environments in oxides derived from the database matches known chemical principles: Cr⁶⁺ prefers tetrahedral (4‑fold) coordination, while Cr³⁺ prefers octahedral (6‑fold) coordination.
Class‑specific computational methodologies and reference reactions are applied for solid‑gas, d‑block oxide, and dissolved‑ion systems to improve agreement with experimental data.

The open‑source software infrastructure of the Materials Project, including pymatgen, has attracted more than 100 active collaborators worldwide and incorporates community contributions such as FEFF and ABINIT support.

Future development plans include adding calculations of surface energies, elastic constants, point defects, finite‑temperature properties, and implementing a two‑way ‘calculations‑on‑demand’ feature for user‑submitted compounds.

The ConvLSTM model accurately predicts fracture patterns, crack‑length trends, and both mode‑I (tensile) and mode‑II (shear) loading responses across crystal orientations, closely matching atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, with only a minor discrepancy for the x100 orientation under mode‑II shear.
The model predicts fracture toughness values that are comparable to those obtained from atomistic molecular dynamics simulations.

A model trained exclusively on single‑crystal data generalizes to bicrystal and gradient‑orientation crystals, reproducing MD fracture patterns for small orientation differences, capturing overall crack paths for large orientation differences, and handling arbitrary geometry gradients.
The ConvLSTM approach reduces computational cost dramatically compared with full molecular dynamics simulations, enabling rapid fracture predictions.
Representing molecular dynamics results as image‑based geometric matrices preserves crystal orientation information and allows the neural network to learn spatiotemporal fracture behavior.
JARVIS-DFT contains approximately 40,000 materials and about 1 million calculated properties.
The integrated JARVIS workflow (DFT → FF → ML) enables rapid screening of materials for high solar‑cell efficiency (SLME) with predictions validated against experimental data.

Machine‑learning models trained on Classical Force‑field Inspired Descriptors (CFID) achieve high predictive accuracy for formation energies, exfoliation energies, band gaps, magnetic moments, refractive indices, dielectric constants, thermoelectric performance, and piezoelectric/infrared modes.
Using the vdW‑DF‑OptB88 functional for all dimensionalities yields accurate lattice parameters and formation energies for both van‑der‑Waals and non‑vdW bonded materials.
The meta‑GGA TBmBJ potential predicts band gaps with accuracy comparable to the hybrid HSE06 functional while requiring up to ten times less computational effort.
Comparisons of JARVIS‑DFT computed formation energies, band gaps, and elastic constants with experimental measurements show acceptable error margins, confirming the database’s predictive reliability.
Beyond‑DFT methods (HSE06, PBE0, G0W0, DMFT) are generated for a subset of materials to provide higher‑level reference data and enable uncertainty quantification.
JARVIS‑FF includes data for roughly 1,500 materials and about 110 classical force‑fields.
JARVIS‑Tools implements automatic k‑point convergence protocols that improve the precision of DFT calculations.
JARVIS‑FF automatically computes bulk modulus, defect formation energies, and phonon spectra for each force‑field and compares them with DFT results to assess force‑field quality.
A REST‑API is provided for programmatic download and upload of JARVIS data, supporting community contributions and interoperability.
Interpretability analyses of JARVIS‑ML models reveal physical insights that go beyond conventional materials‑science intuition.
The computational cost of LiFlow scales linearly with the number of atoms (O(n)), in contrast to the cubic scaling (O(n³)) of ab initio molecular dynamics.

Incorporating an adaptive, thermally and chemically conditioned Maxwell–Boltzmann prior markedly lowers mean absolute errors and raises rank correlations for MSD and RDF compared with an isotropic prior; ablation studies show performance degradation without it.
Incorporating the Corrector model reduces RDF mean absolute error and mitigates large‑displacement artifacts, improving MSD prediction across temperatures, especially for hydrogen diffusion.
Within the training temperature range, LiFlow’s predicted diffusivity D* closely matches reference values from Winter and Gómez‑Bombarelli.
When extrapolating to temperatures lower than the training range, LiFlow’s predicted diffusivity D* decreases more slowly than reference data, indicating fictitious diffusive behavior at high 1000/T.
The adaptive prior classifier provides limited benefit at the lowest temperature (600 K), reducing its overall effectiveness under that condition.
A curated dataset of 476 binary ionic compound melting temperatures spanning 0-4,000°C was compiled for machine learning model development.
The best one-step gradient-boosted tree regression model achieves 165±4 K MAE and 0.89 R² on the test set for melting temperature prediction.
A two-step approach combining unsupervised clustering with supervised regression achieves 156±4 K MAE and 0.92 R², outperforming direct one-step supervised learning.
Cluster 1 (198 compounds, mostly ionic halides and oxides) achieves 136±5 K MAE and 0.92 R², while Cluster 2 (222 compounds, mostly covalent carbides and nitrides) achieves 189±7 K MAE and 0.90 R².
Cohesive energy and elastic moduli (shear and bulk modulus) are the most important features for melting temperature prediction, as identified by both ensemble feature importance and SHAP analysis.
Models trained without elastic moduli features yield errors greater than 400 K, demonstrating that elastic features are necessary for accurate melting temperature predictions.
Very-high melting temperatures (>3150 K) appear only in Cluster 2, predominantly in metal carbides, reflecting the covalent bonding character of these materials.

Tree ensemble methods (gradient-boosted trees and random forest regression) substantially outperform linear models, which achieve MAE >240 K and RMSE >340 K, at least 100 K worse than non-linear approaches.

The two-step clustering approach provides interpretability by revealing different melting physics dominated by bonding types, with Cluster 1 governed by ionic bonding features and Cluster 2 by covalent bonding features.

Cluster 2 melting temperatures can be accurately represented with symbolic models depending on only two features: squared cohesive energy and inverse square root of periodic groups or electronegativities.
The featurization methods are transferable to more complex compositions, enabling new ML models to be fitted without revising the materials embedding method given extended datasets.
CHGNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Matbench Discovery benchmark, outperforming eight other submitted models.

On the Materials Project Trajectory test set, CHGNet trained with magnetic moment labels attains mean absolute errors of 30 meV/atom for energy, 77 meV/Å for forces, 0.348 GPa for stress, and 0.032 µB for magnetic moments.

CHGNet molecular dynamics simulations of Li superionic conductors reproduce room‑temperature ionic conductivities and activation energies within the error bars of AIMD, correctly distinguishing faster from slower conductors.
CHGNet integrates magnetic moment labels as a proxy for atomic charge, enabling inference of atomic charges and accurate differentiation of oxidation states such as V³⁺/V⁴⁺ and Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺.

In charge‑informed molecular dynamics of Li₀.₅MnO₂ at 1100 K, CHGNet predicts the emergence of Mn²⁺ after ~0.8 ns, coinciding with a ~50 meV/oxygen reduction in potential energy and the formation of a spinel‑like phase, indicating a correlation between charge disproportionation and phase transformation.

Including electronic entropy via charge‑decorated cluster expansions, CHGNet reproduces the experimentally observed miscibility gap and eutectoid‑like transition in the LiₓFePO₄ phase diagram, whereas a non‑charge‑decorated model fails to capture these features.
Fine‑tuning the pretrained CHGNet on the Li‑Fe‑P‑O chemical space reduces the test error from 23 meV/atom to 15 meV/atom.
CHGNet captures long‑range interactions up to 20 Å with only four atom‑convolution layers while maintaining low computational cost.
CHGNet enables nanosecond‑scale molecular dynamics simulations of garnet Li₃La₃Te₂O₁₂, yielding lithium self‑diffusion coefficients with quantified uncertainty.
Using magnetic moments as a charge proxy does not strictly ensure global charge neutrality in CHGNet predictions.

The Materials Project Trajectory dataset used to pre‑train CHGNet contains approximately 1.58 million atomic configurations spanning 94 elements, with magnetic moment labels for 76 elements, providing comprehensive chemical coverage.
Continuous-filter convolutional (cfconv) layers enable convolution on arbitrarily positioned inputs, overcoming the limitations of discrete filters that require grid-aligned data.

On the ISO17 benchmark, SchNet reaches chemical‑accuracy (≈0.5 kcal/mol MAE) for energy predictions on molecules seen during training and further improves predictions on unseen isomers when forces are included in training.
Including force information in the training loss causally improves SchNet’s generalization to previously unseen chemical structures in ISO17.
GDML cannot be trained on 50,000 MD17 examples due to its quadratic scaling with the number of atoms and samples, whereas SchNet scales to that dataset size.
The ISO17 benchmark, comprising 645,000 conformations of 129 C7O2H10 isomers, is introduced to evaluate models on combined chemical and conformational variation.
Using a shifted softplus activation guarantees an infinitely differentiable (smooth) potential energy surface, facilitating geometry optimization.
Continuous-filter convolutions produce smoother energy predictions than discrete filters, as illustrated in Figure 1.
On the QM9 benchmark, SchNet attains a mean absolute error of 0.31 kcal/mol for total‑energy prediction with 110 k training examples, outperforming DTNN (0.84) and enn‑s2s (0.45).

Non-conservative (unconstrained) MLIP models consistently show 2-3× theoretical speed-up over their conservative counterparts, with direct force prediction providing additional 2-3× speedup compared to forces computed via automatic differentiation.

The PET architecture scales to 730M parameters (OMat-XL) while maintaining tractable memory usage and computational efficiency due to increased node representation size and unconstrained architecture.
Conservative PET-OAM models achieve state-of-the-art performance on phonon tasks in matbench-discovery and the best overall accuracy in predicting shear modulus among tested models.

Non-conservative models allow residual asymmetries to drive relaxation toward more stable close-packed structures, unlike equivariant models that remain trapped in symmetric but unstable configurations, though 70% (16%) of final configurations retain symmetry of initial structure with 0.01 Å threshold for conservative (non-conservative) models.

Elastic moduli predictions are very sensitive to the lack of energy conservation in MLIP models, and non-conservative models consistently perform worse on matbench-discovery downstream tasks despite achieving better training and validation accuracies.

Central finite differences can more than halve the error for non-equivariant models on phonon calculations by averaging out inconsistencies between symmetry-equivalent displacements, and O(3)-averaging increases symmetric structures to 77% with symprec 0.01 Å in the non-conservative case.

DFT setting inconsistency between training and evaluation datasets significantly affects MLIP model performance comparisons, with PET-OMAD performing worse than PET-OAM and PET-MPtrj on Inorganic Materials due to differences in ab initio theory levels.

The PET-OMat model series spans a broad range of cost/accuracy tradeoff scenarios from 4.5M to 730M parameters, with pre-trained models released covering diverse chemical systems across the full periodic table.
Universal MLIPs trained on massive datasets can generalize across diverse chemical systems and can be successfully applied to structural optimization and lattice dynamics workflows.
UMLIPs trained on the MatPES dataset achieve test mean absolute errors in energies that are 4–10 times lower than UMLIPs trained on the larger MPRelax or OMat24 datasets.

Across equilibrium, near‑equilibrium, and molecular‑dynamics property benchmarks, MatPES‑trained UMLIPs match or surpass the performance of models trained on much larger datasets such as OMat24 (≈100 M structures).
Molecular‑dynamics simulations using MatPES‑trained UMLIPs exhibit markedly higher stability, with median termination temperatures up to ~1,900 K, versus ~1,300–1,500 K for MPRelax and OMat24 models.

On near‑equilibrium benchmarks, MatPES UMLIPs significantly improve the prediction of shear modulus (G_VRH) and off‑equilibrium forces while achieving similar bulk‑modulus (K_VRH) and heat‑capacity (C_V) accuracy compared to MPRelax and OMat24 models.
TensorNet‑MatPES predicts ionic conductivities of Li/Na solid electrolytes with high fidelity (positive R²), whereas TensorNet‑MPF severely overestimates conductivities and yields a negative R².

The MatPES v2025.1 dataset contains 504,811 structures (434,712 PBE and 387,897 r2SCAN calculations) sampled from a configuration space of ~281 million MD snapshots and ~16 billion atomic environments.
The 2DIRECT sampling workflow yields a data‑efficient dataset that, despite being a fraction of the size of MPRelax, samples a substantially larger region of structural and atomic‑environment space.
The r2SCAN functional provides a more accurate description of interatomic bonding than PBE, leading to improved potential‑energy‑surface quality in the MatPES r2SCAN dataset.

Training a TensorNet model on the 400 k‑structure MatPES‑PBE dataset requires approximately 15 minutes per epoch on a single RTX A6000 GPU, whereas training on the 100 M‑structure OMat24 dataset needs about 20 hours per epoch on sixteen A100 GPUs, highlighting the computational efficiency of MatPES.
TransIP achieves SO(3) equivariance through training with a contrastive latent equivariance objective rather than hard-wired equivariant architectural constraints.
A generic unconstrained Transformer can serve as an effective backbone for machine-learned interatomic potentials without explicit equivariance constraints.
TransIP achieves 40% to 60% improvement in performance compared to data augmentation baseline (TransAug) across varying OMol25 dataset sizes.
In the limited data regime (1M samples), TransIP achieves 255 meV/Å force MAE versus 600 meV/Å for TransAug, with force cosine similarity of 0.7 versus 0.44.
TransIP achieves 58 meV/atom energy MAE compared to TransAug's 120 meV/atom at 1M training samples.
TransIP-S and TransIP-M achieve significantly faster inference than eSEN baseline at 160,000 and 70,000 atoms/sec versus 15,000 atoms/sec respectively.
A 48% reduction in equivariance error from 1M to 4M training examples translates to 40-60% performance improvements, exceeding what would be expected from data scaling alone.
TransIP learns an embedding where input rotations act approximately as a shared orthogonal transformation across different molecules despite no explicit equivariance in the architecture.
TransIP scales smoothly with parameter count while TransAug exhibits poorer scaling with larger models performing worse than smaller ones.
TransIP uses a single-stage training pipeline without requiring separate pretraining-finetuning framework or explicit equivariance constraints.

The Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance on all QM9 regression targets, reaching chemical accuracy on 11 of the 13 targets and outperforming prior models such as SchNet and DTNN.
The multiple‑tower architecture reduces the computational complexity of a propagation step from O(n²d²) to O(n²d²/k) and yields a 2× speedup for n=9, d=200, k=8.
A general training method allows MPNNs to use larger node representation dimensions without increasing computation time or memory, providing substantial savings over previous high‑dimensional MPNNs.
Adding a latent master node that connects to every atom provides a global scratch space, allowing larger hidden dimensions with minimal performance penalty.
Using a pair‑message function that depends on both source and destination node states improves message‑passing efficiency compared with the standard matrix‑multiplication message function.
The Message Passing Neural Network framework unifies eight previously proposed graph‑based neural models under a single formalism.
Learning directly from molecular graphs without handcrafted descriptors enables the MPNN to achieve lower prediction errors than descriptor‑based methods.
Across all QM9 properties, the MPNN reduces the mean absolute error by 30–70 % relative to the best previously reported graph‑neural‑network baseline.

For internal energy at 0 K (U0), enthalpy (H), Gibbs free energy (G), heat capacity at constant volume (Cv), and highest vibrational frequency (Ω), the MPNN records lower mean absolute errors than SchNet and DTNN (U0 MAE 0.45 vs 0.55/0.72; H 0.39 vs 0.59/0.80; G 0.44 vs 0.55/0.74; Cv 0.80 vs 0.99/1.71; Ω 0.19 vs 0.41/0.78).
Standard Gaussian quadrature rules produce frame‑dependent (non‑objective) phase‑averaged internal energies for rotated crystal lattices.
Gaussian quadrature leads to abrupt energy jumps and fictitious minima when neighbor cut‑off radii change during large deformations.
Fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature yields internal energies and free‑energy curves that remain in good agreement with molecular dynamics results across the full temperature range studied.
An E(3)‑equivariant graph neural network architecture guarantees rotational invariance of predicted phase‑averaged quantities.

The E(3)‑equivariant GNN surrogate provides superior accuracy compared with third‑ and fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature for thermal expansion of copper, martensitic phase transition of iron, and grain‑boundary energy calculations, matching molecular dynamics reference data.
The GNN surrogate achieves mean absolute errors of ≤0.313 meV for energy, ≤0.189 meV/Å for forces, and ≤0.0734 meV/Å² for thermal forces on validation sets.

Inference with the trained GNN is significantly faster than evaluating fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature, enabling frequent high‑dimensional integral evaluations and quasistatic finite‑temperature atomistic simulations without costly MD averaging.
The GNN‑assisted integration framework can be applied to high‑dimensional integration problems beyond atomistics.
DeePMD-kit supports multiple atomic descriptor types including local frame, DeepPot-SE, attention-based, and hybrid descriptors.

The DeepPot-SE descriptor is continuous up to the second-order derivative in its domain, unlike the local frame descriptor which is not smooth at the cutoff radius and when exchanging the order of two nearest neighbors.
None of the tested descriptors outperforms the others in terms of accuracy across all datasets.
Compressed models are 1x-10x faster than the original models for both training and inference.
NVNMD (non-von Neumann molecular dynamics) is 50x-100x faster than regular MD simulations.
FP32 precision is 0.5x to 2x faster than FP64 precision in nearly all tested systems while demonstrating similar validation errors.
The DPLR model adds electrostatic energy to the total energy, with electrostatic energy calculated in Fourier space for modeling long-range interactions.
The fitting network can fit potential energy, force, virial, and tensorial properties such as dipole and polarizability.
Model deviation is defined as the standard deviation of properties inferred by an ensemble of models trained with independently initialized parameters.
DeePMD-kit APIs have been integrated into multiple third-party MD packages including LAMMPS, i-PI, GROMACS, AMBER, OpenMM, and ABACUS.
DeePMD-kit supports interpolation between Deep Potential models and empirical pairwise potentials for cases where DFT calculations fail at close interatomic distances.
DeePMD-kit has added MPI implementation for multi-device training and MD simulations using Horovod for data-parallel distributed training.
DeePMD-kit can simulate systems containing almost all periodic table elements including drug-like molecules, ions, transition states, and excited states.

Latent Ewald Summation cannot infer correct partial charges without reference charge labels and frequently predicts charges near zero or opposite in sign to reference values in challenging chemical environments such as MOFs.
Baseline versions of MACE and Allegro are degenerate with respect to total charge and cannot distinguish between molecules with different charge states without long-range corrections.

Biased train-test splitting strategies including cluster, maximal separation, size, and random splits enable rigorous benchmarking by explicitly testing model performance in significantly different regions of chemical space.
EFA enables modeling of long-range interactions without requiring explicit neighbor cutoffs and outperforms CELLI on most benchmarking subsplits when reference charges are unavailable.

MACE without long-range correction does not generalize well to out-of-distribution samples, while integration of long-range correction schemes has significant effects on both MACE and Allegro architectures.

Metal-organic frameworks present an ideal application for MLIPs because classical force fields lack required accuracy while DFT is too computationally expensive for large unit cells and long timescales.

Total charge embeddings can recover much of CELLI's performance on some datasets but generalize poorly in size-based extrapolation and should be viewed as a potential extension rather than replacement for long-range methods.
The observed improvements from long-range corrections cannot be attributed to increased model capacity as all variants share identical hyperparameters and nearly identical parameter counts.
EFA and CELLI do not lead to improvements when no reference charges are provided in the ODAC25 dataset.
Foundational MLIP models often fail to outperform simple classical force fields for MOF systems without long-range corrections.
NequIP outperforms kernel‑based approaches such as sGDML and FCHL19/GPR across benchmarks, including small-data regimes and the MD-17 dataset.
NequIP requires up to three orders of magnitude fewer training configurations than existing neural interatomic potentials to reach comparable accuracy.
When trained on only 133 structures (~1 k frames), NequIP outperforms DeepMD trained on 133,500 structures for liquid water and ice simulations.
Using higher-order E(3)-equivariant representations (increasing rotation order from l=0 to l=1 and up to l=3) consistently reduces prediction error and improves accuracy across all evaluated tasks.
Predicting forces as the negative gradient of the learned total energy guarantees energy conservation and rotation‑equivariant forces.
The equivariant architecture scales linearly with the number of atoms because convolutions are limited to a local cutoff radius.
NequIP reproduces structural and kinetic properties from ab‑initio molecular dynamics simulations with high fidelity.
xDeepH accurately reproduces DFT band structures of (16,16) CrI3 nanotubes for both non‑collinear surface‑normal magnetization and collinear ferromagnetism.
xDeepH accurately predicts the band structure of monolayer NiBr2 with a 19×1×1 spin‑spiral magnetic order, matching DFT results.
Introducing magnetic moments via a strictly localized magnetic‑moment layer yields more efficient and accurate training than treating atomic and magnetic structures on equal footing.
The ENN architecture of xDeepH preserves equivariance under the Euclidean and time‑reversal symmetry group E(3)×{I,T}, which is essential for the method's performance.

The presence of a magnetic skyrmion in Moiré‑twisted CrI3 removes an extremely flat valence band that appears in the ferromagnetic configuration, indicating strong coupling between the flat band and the skyrmion.
The PBE functional combined with PAW potentials is the default exchange-correlation functional and potential combination for ICSD, Binary Alloy, and Heusler databases.
The applied plane-wave kinetic energy cut-off (Ecut) is the largest recommended value among all species in the calculation, increased by a factor of 1.4.
DFT+U corrections are applied to the entire ICSD database and certain Heusler database entries containing O, S, Se, and F elements, but not to the Binary Alloy database.

Specific Ueff parameters are defined for d-block elements (Table 4) and U, J parameters for f-block elements (Table 5) to correct self-interaction error in DFT+U calculations, with values ranging from 1.9 eV (In) to 7.5 eV (Zn).

The first RELAX calculation is performed in collinear spin-polarized fashion with initial magnetic moments set to 1.0 µB per atom, and spin polarization is turned off in subsequent calculations if magnetization is below 0.025 µB/atom.

Electronic convergence criteria are δEelec = 10⁻⁵ eV and ionic convergence criteria are δEion = 10⁻⁴ eV for Elements database entries, while all other databases use δEelec = 10⁻³ eV and δEion = 10⁻² eV.

Following the AFLOW standard enables materials science researchers to reproduce AFLOWLIB consortium results and make direct comparisons of properties between different materials for identifying trends and formulating design rules.
The AFLOWLIB data is accessible through a REST-API for standardized data exchange.
For bulk elastic constants (B, C11, C12, C44) the GAP model achieves fractional errors of less than 10% relative to DFT, outperforming all other evaluated interatomic potentials.
Surface energies of the (111), (110) and (100) silicon cleavage planes are predicted by GAP with errors of around 2% relative to DFT, which is comparable or better than other potentials.
Formation energies of vacancy and interstitial point defects (hexagonal, tetrahedral, dumbbell) are predicted by GAP within 10% of DFT values, providing uniform accuracy across these defects.

For extrapolative planar defects not included in the training set—specifically the (112) Σ3 grain boundary and unstable stacking fault energies on the (111) shuffle and glide planes—GAP errors remain within 20% of DFT, outperforming other models.
Combining a simple repulsive pair potential with a many‑body SOAP‑kernel term in the GAP framework yields meV‑per‑atom accuracy for silicon energetics.

Using the GAP model enables simulations that would be prohibitively expensive with DFT, such as finite‑temperature phase‑boundary calculations, liquid self‑diffusivity, amorphous silicon formation by slow quench, and dynamic brittle fracture.

A training database of manageable size, constructed from DFT configurations covering relevant phases and defects, is sufficient to achieve high transferability of the GAP model across diverse silicon configurations.
Benchmark comparisons show that the new GAP model yields lower errors than previous GAP models for silicon.
The Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) kernel captures the regularity of the silicon potential energy surface, leading to accurate interpolation within the sampled configuration space.
Orb-v3 and SevenNet classify materials as good versus bad ionic conductors with accuracy greater than 82% using a 500 meV migration barrier threshold.
All MLIPs struggle with high migration barrier predictions, with only 3.7-20.7% achieving acceptable accuracy (<0.1 eV error) in the 1.31-2.50 eV range.
MACE-MP-0 and SevenNet intermediate images provide better initial guesses relative to conventional interpolation techniques in over 71% of structures.
M3GNet and CHGNet exhibit systematic bias toward underestimating migration barriers, with 73.1% and 78.2% of predictions being underestimates respectively.
In the low-barrier range of 0.0025-0.25 eV, more than 50% of predictions achieve acceptable accuracy across all MLIPs tested.
IDPP interpolation does not make a significant difference in enhancing the initial guess for the minimum energy path compared to linear interpolation across all MLIPs.
Orb-v3 and SevenNet are suitable for high-throughput screening of candidate battery materials based on their >82% classification accuracy for ionic conductors.

Matbench v0.1 is a benchmark suite containing 13 supervised machine learning tasks (10 regression, 3 classification) for materials property prediction, with dataset sizes ranging from 312 to 132,752 samples.

Matbench contains data from 10 density functional theory-derived and experimental sources including Materials Project, Zhuo et al., Landolt-Bornstein Handbook, Castelli et al., JARVIS DFT 2D, and Citrine Informatics.

Automatminer is a fully-automated machine learning pipeline consisting of four stages (autofeaturization, cleaning, dimensionality reduction, and AutoML search) that requires no user intervention or hyperparameter tuning.

Graph network models (CGCNN and MEGNet) have high errors on small datasets (<10^4 samples) but leverage large datasets more efficiently, outperforming traditional ML and AutoML approaches on tasks with approximately 10^4 data points or more.

Descriptor-based Automatminer and RF models have lower errors on small datasets but their improvement rates are shallower, with AutoML's advantage over conventional techniques narrowing as sample count increases and essentially lost near 10^5 samples.
All algorithms exhibit a universal trend of decreasing relative errors as dataset size increases.

For small datasets (<10^4 samples), inexpensive Automatminer presets (~1-5 minute training) retain the bulk of performance compared to expensive presets (24h+ training), with Express retaining 95% or more of the accuracy of more expensive presets at less than 50% of the computational cost on data-scarce tasks.

Graph networks (CGCNN and MEGNet) far outperform traditional ML algorithms on formation energy prediction tasks, with MEGNet decisively outperforming Automatminer for the PhDOS task; among nine structure-based tasks, Automatminer and MEGNet each achieve best scores on 4 tasks.

Matbench provides a consistent evaluation framework using five-fold nested cross-validation on identical folds across all algorithms to minimize comparison bias, with datasets pre-cleaned to remove unphysical computed data and task-irrelevant experimental data.
Automatminer source code and pre-processed Matbench tasks are open source and available online.

The frozen-framework PES descriptor screening ranks lithium-containing Materials Project compounds such that eight of the ten highest‑ranked materials are confirmed to be room‑temperature superionic conductors by first‑principles calculations.

The proposed screening method is approximately 50 × faster than molecular dynamics driven by a machine‑learning interatomic potential and at least 3 000 × faster than first‑principles molecular dynamics.

AIMD simulations of the five top‑Ξ candidates confirm high ionic conductivities (e.g., Li(BH)6 shows σ ≈ 0.9 S cm⁻¹ at 1000 K with activation energy 219 ± 86 meV), validating the screening predictions.

The screening pipeline, when applied to 5 997 lithium‑containing Materials Project structures that satisfy basic stability and band‑gap criteria, yields 1302 structures after removing transition‑metal containing compounds, of which 113 have Ξ > 0.25.
All evaluated descriptors (MPE, FV‑connected, FV‑disconnected) achieve ranking scores above those of a random‑guess classifier, demonstrating predictive capability for ionic conductivity.

Finite‑size tests using a larger supercell and an ML‑IAP (SevenNet) show that diffusion coefficients converge within statistical uncertainties, confirming that the AIMD results are not significantly affected by supercell size.
The Ξ descriptor screening increases the proportion of room‑temperature superionic candidates from ~7% in an unbiased sample to 55% in the top‑100 Ξ‑ranked list, an ~8‑fold improvement.
SevenNet‑driven MD ranks LiB3H8 as having the highest extrapolated room‑temperature conductivity, roughly an order of magnitude larger than the reference Li7P3S11.
Hydroborate structures appear at the top of the Ξ‑ordered list despite not being present in the training datasets, demonstrating the method’s generalization capability.
All AIMD‑tested structures are diffusive at 1000 K, and 88 % of the top‑100 Ξ‑selected materials are diffusive in the SevenNet‑driven MD validation.

Computing the frozen‑framework PES descriptors for 5997 Materials Project structures required seven days on a 48‑core CPU with two RTX 6000 GPUs, comparable to the time needed for ML‑driven MD on 100 materials.
Selecting structures by the Ξ ranking descriptor markedly enriches the sample with high ionic conductivity at 1000 K, 500 K, and extrapolated room temperature compared with a random selection.
Mean‑square‑displacement (MSD) slopes obtained from SevenNet‑driven MD agree closely with those from ab‑initio AIMD, demonstrating consistency between the two simulation approaches.

Using an ML‑trained interatomic potential (ML‑IAP) enables validation of many more candidate structures than conventional AIMD, as demonstrated by MD simulations on 30 random and 100 top‑Ξ structures.

Artificial intelligence has transformed multiscale modeling by linking atomic, mesoscale, and continuum scales, delivering improved accuracy and reduced computational cost compared with traditional methods.

Machine‑learning‑driven interatomic potentials (e.g., GAP, DeePMD) and DFT‑trained surrogate models enable simulations of up to millions of atoms while retaining accuracy close to first‑principles benchmarks, making large‑scale high‑fidelity simulations feasible.

Neural‑network‑based electronic‑structure prediction tools achieve significant speedups over conventional density‑functional theory while maintaining comparable accuracy, accelerating electronic‑structure calculations.

Integrating renormalization‑group concepts with machine‑learning architectures has been used to predict transitions to canted antiferromagnetic phases in 3D Ising and Fermi‑Hubbard models, to classify quantum phases, and to recognize complex many‑body phases from raw simulation data.
Current challenges limiting AI‑driven multiscale modeling include limited data availability, restricted model transferability, and limited explainability.
Future integration of formal renormalization‑group concepts with machine‑learning architectures is a promising direction for modeling systems near criticality or with strong electron correlations.

OMat24 comprises over 118 million DFT calculations across diverse chemistries, materials, and configurations for inorganic bulk materials, making it up to 2 orders of magnitude larger than other openly available datasets in terms of number of single-point calculations.

OMat24 exhibits more uniform and comprehensive coverage of near-neighbor pairs and element distributions compared to both Alexandria and MPtrj datasets, with elemental coverage spanning most of the periodic table.

OMat24 contains a large fraction of far-from-equilibrium structures with 1 to 100 atoms per structure (majority having less than 20 atoms), yielding broader label distributions than relaxation-only datasets.

MLIP models trained on OMat24 achieve F1 scores above 0.9 for stability prediction and 20 meV/atom accuracy for formation energy on Matbench Discovery, with all five top-performing models on the Matbench Discovery leaderboard exclusively trained on OMat24.

OMat24's diversity corrects the systematic softening bias of prior models trained on less diverse datasets, with systematic softening improvements across all degrees consistently observed in five distinct architectures, indicating the effect is largely architecture-independent.
Training on OMat24 results in models with better extrapolation to regions with lower dataset density farther away from the convex hull compared to models trained on other datasets.

The mean absolute difference in formation energies between MP and OMat24 DFT settings is 13.5 meV/atom across 423 compounds, with differences largely attributed to different versions of pseudo-potentials and different pseudo-potential symbols for Yb and W.

The mean absolute error between DFT predicted and experimental formation energies for 222 compounds is 55 meV/atom using OMat24 DFT settings, with compatibility corrections computed following the Materials Project MP2020 Compatibility scheme.
Machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on OMat24 predict tightly converged DFT forces with accuracy comparable to or better than predictions for less tightly converged calculations.

A two-step training strategy with direct force pretraining followed by conservative finetuning results in eSEN models with higher accuracy requiring less total training epochs and time compared to training conservative models from scratch.

The diversity of the larger OMat24 dataset does not benefit from the regularization or augmentation provided by DeNS, whereas dataset augmentation techniques like DeNS can significantly enhance performance when training solely on the MPtraj dataset.
For the eSEN architecture, prediction error plateaus at approximately 100 million samples, matching the total size of the OMat24 training set.
DeepH predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements for graphene with an average mean absolute error of 2.1 meV and a coefficient of determination r² = 0.9994 across all orbital combinations.
For monolayer MoS₂, DeepH predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements with average mean absolute errors of 1.3 meV (Mo–Mo), 1.0 meV (Mo–S), 0.7 meV (S–Mo), and 0.8 meV (S–S).
Band structures and electric susceptibility computed from DeepH for MoS₂ match DFT results closely.
DeepH generalizes to carbon nanotubes, achieving Hamiltonian prediction MAE below 3.5 meV for diameters larger than 2 nm and accurately reproducing their band structures.
DeepH scales linearly with system size and provides a three‑order‑of‑magnitude speed‑up over conventional DFT for a MoS₂ 35 × 35 supercell.

A DeepH model trained only on non‑twisted bilayer graphene structures predicts Hamiltonians for twisted bilayer graphene supercells up to ~1000 atoms with sub‑meV mean absolute error and correctly reproduces the flat‑band feature near the Fermi level at the magic angle (~1.08°).
Compared with empirical tight‑binding and continuum models, DeepH offers higher accuracy and transferability for twisted van‑der‑Waals materials, albeit with slightly lower computational efficiency.
DeepH resolves the accuracy‑efficiency dilemma of DFT, enabling efficient ab‑initio electronic‑structure calculations for large‑scale material systems.
The use of a local‑coordinate message‑passing (LCMP) layer is critical for achieving high prediction accuracy of rotation‑covariant Hamiltonian blocks.

DeepH can be applied to both periodic and non‑periodic systems, including three‑dimensional bulk carbon allotropes and quasi‑zero‑dimensional molecules, achieving sub‑meV mean absolute error for Hamiltonian predictions.
Phonax efficiently predicts phonon dispersion relations and density of states for inorganic crystal materials.
Augmenting a minimal 1×1×1 supercell training set with Hessian data yields more accurate phonon predictions than training on a larger 3×3×3 supercell alone.
Fine‑tuning an energy model on a benzene vibrational spectrum improves spectrum predictions for unseen molecules such as toluene and phenol.
A generalized energy model that includes external electric‑field dependence can predict polarization, Born effective charges, and polarizability, and improves energy and force MAE.
The Phonax framework works for both periodic crystals and isolated molecules and can be extended to higher‑order derivatives such as field‑dependent properties.

The QR‑based reparameterization used in D4FT preserves the orthonormal constraints of Kohn‑Sham orbitals, making the search space equivalent to the original orthogonal function space, as proved in Proposition 3.1, and can be interpreted as projected gradient descent on the orthogonal constraint set.

Direct minimization of the total KS‑DFT energy with stochastic gradient descent reduces the asymptotic computational complexity from O(N⁴) to O(N³), and the full‑batch D4FT algorithm has complexity O(nN²)+O(n²N²), which is lower than the O(n²N²) complexity of conventional SCF; minibatch training further lowers the cost.
Across a benchmark set ranging from He to benzene, D4FT reproduces ground‑state energies of the reference PySCF implementation with deviations ≤0.02 Ha (LSDA/6‑31g and LSDA/STO‑3g).
D4FT correctly predicts the paramagnetic ground state of O₂ and the diamagnetic ground state of CO₂ by comparing spin‑restricted and spin‑unrestricted calculations.
D4FT converges faster than JAX‑SCF, demonstrating a smaller computational complexity and reduced number of iterations.
D4FT provides a unified optimization algorithm with a stronger convergence guarantee than traditional SCF fixed‑point iteration.
D4FT successfully converges on unstable fullerene fragments (C₁₂₀, C₁₄₀) where PySCF fails to converge within the default iteration limit.

Standard numerical integration based on truncated series expansions may incur large truncation errors for fully neural wave functions, suggesting Monte Carlo integration as a more suitable alternative.
Orb-v3 achieves near state-of-the-art performance across evaluations with at least 10x reduction in latency and 8x reduction in memory compared to alternative MLIPs.
Orb-v3-direct-20 uses only 32.8GB GPU memory for 100,000 atom systems and completes in under half a second, while all baseline methods and conservative models encounter Out Of Memory errors.
Orb-v3-direct-* models are the only universal MLIPs that can compute hundreds of forward passes per second, exceeding one million steps per hour for small systems.
Orb-v3-direct-20-omat is comparable in accuracy to current state-of-the-art models while being approximately 30 times faster than SevenNet.
Only orb-v3-conservative-inf is truly energy-conserving in NVE molecular dynamics simulations; all other Orb-v3 variants exhibit energy drift.
Equigrad regularization improves rotational invariance of Orb-v3 by approximately 5x compared to default loss training.
Distillation from conservative models resolves direct models' tendency to overfit to forces and struggle with second- and third-order PES derivatives when trained on mpa datasets.
Graph construction routines can dominate runtime for state-of-the-art MLIPs, requiring efficient off-the-shelf solutions for extreme scalability.
Foundation models enable cross-domain generalization and emergent capabilities for scientific discovery in materials science.
GNoME discovered over 2.2 million new stable inorganic materials and more than 45 000 new crystal prototypes, an order‑of‑magnitude increase over prior discovery efforts.
MACE‑MP‑0 attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for periodic systems while preserving equivariant inductive biases.

Multimodal models such as nach0, MultiMat, and MatterChat demonstrate reasoning over combined structural, textual, and spectral data, whereas most current foundation models remain unimodal and lack integrated image, spectrum, and experimental‑metadata fusion.

LLM‑based agents such as HoneyComb, LLMatDesign, ChatMOF, MatAgent, and MatPilot have been developed to automate literature search, hypothesis generation, synthesis planning, and experimental verification in materials science.

Existing materials datasets are heavily skewed toward inorganic atomistic systems, with limited coverage of polymers, composites, and mesoscale phenomena, creating a critical data imbalance for foundation‑model training.

Future research should focus on scalable pretraining, continual learning, data governance, trustworthiness, and incorporation of physics‑informed constraints such as equivariance, quantum‑mechanical symmetries, and thermodynamic principles to improve accuracy, interpretability, and trustworthiness of foundation models.

The autonomous A‑Lab platform synthesized 41 of 58 targeted materials (71 % success) over a 17‑day experiment with minimal human intervention, demonstrating high‑throughput autonomous materials synthesis.

Benchmarks such as LLM4Mat‑Bench, MaCBench, and MatBench evaluate multiple models across millions of structures and dozens of properties, revealing significant performance differences and that domain‑specific pretraining yields substantial improvements on materials‑science tasks like property prediction and named‑entity recognition.

MatterSim, a zero‑shot machine‑learned interatomic potential trained on >17 million DFT‑labeled structures, supports universal simulation across all elements, temperatures and pressures, achieving energy prediction errors below 50 meV/atom even in high‑temperature, non‑equilibrium regimes.
SevenNet achieves over 80% parallel efficiency in weak-scaling scenarios on a 32-GPU cluster with SiO2 benchmarks.
SevenNet-0 achieves mean absolute errors of 24 meV/atom for energy, 0.067 eV/Å for force, and 0.65 GPa for stress on the test set.
The parallelization algorithm restricts communication range between neighboring processors to the original cutoff radius (rc) rather than rc multiplied by message-passing steps.
SevenNet-0 successfully generated amorphous Si3N4 structure with 112,000 atoms through melt-quench MD simulation, reproducing key structural features matching DFT reference data.
The melt-quench simulation with 112,000 atoms on 8 GPUs demonstrated 0.94 parallel efficiency compared to single-GPU baseline.
SevenNet-0 shows improvements in energy and force accuracies compared to M3GNet (35 meV/atom, 0.072 eV/Å).
Architecture modifications reduced SevenNet-0 total model parameters from 16.24 million (GNoME) to 0.84 million.
SevenNet exhibits nearly ideal strong-scaling performance as long as GPUs are fully utilized.
Strong-scaling performance significantly declines with suboptimal GPU utilization, particularly for lightweight models or simulations with small numbers of atoms.
SevenNet-0, trained solely on crystal structures, reproduced key structural features of amorphous Si3N4 including fourfold coordination for Si and threefold coordination for N atoms.
A 60-ps MD simulation with 112,000 atoms using SevenNet-0 required 12.7 hours, approximately 0.1 ns per day.
SevenNet interfaces with the LAMMPS package for MD simulations using TorchScript to integrate trained models.
The parallelization algorithm is applicable to GNN-IP models using two-body message-passing functions including SchNet, PhysNet, PaiNN, NequIP, and MACE.

The DeePMD model successfully reproduces the superionic behavior of solid-state electrolytes with linear Lithium/Sodium mean squared displacement over time and diffusion coefficient uncertainty of about 20% or smaller, which is precise enough for battery applications.
For LLZO, the computed activation energies range from 0.2 to 0.22 eV, in very good agreement with experimental values of 0.20-0.21 eV for cubic LLZO.
For NASICON, training starting from FPMD configurations with 80 atoms fails to converge even after three training loops with activation energies spanning 0.2-0.4 eV.

Training set cleaning procedures including minimum ion-ion distance cutoff, energy/force outlier removal, and loss condition monitoring are necessary to help the algorithm converge to a physical model.

The proposed training protocol based on augmenting the training set via intermediate molecular dynamics simulations can assess the quality of approximate trajectories and computed physical properties.
The DeePMD model is a promising candidate for developing a universal potential for solid-state electrolytes, though care must be taken when selecting training configurations.
For LLZO, results are quite insensitive to the choice of cell volume (NPT equilibrated vs experimental cif-file values) for producing the initial training set.
The number of force components in the initial training set is more important than total configurations for obtaining generalizable models.

Simple MEGNet models that use only atomic number and spatial distance as input achieve chemical accuracy, perform comparably to full‑feature models, and outperform prior state‑of‑the‑art models on 8 of the 13 QM9 properties.

MEGNet models trained on approximately 60,000 crystals outperform prior models (SchNet and CGCNN) for formation energy, band gap, bulk modulus, and shear modulus, achieving errors comparable to or better than density‑functional‑theory uncertainties.

A unified free‑energy MEGNet model that incorporates temperature, pressure, and entropy as global state inputs predicts U₀, U, H, and G with a combined mean absolute error of 0.010 eV, comparable to separate single‑property models.

Elemental embedding vectors learned by the crystal formation‑energy MEGNet model reproduce known periodic‑table trends and, when transferred to band‑gap and elastic‑moduli models, reduce their mean absolute errors, improving upon prior machine‑learning approaches.
Ensembling two independently trained three‑block MEGNet models lowers the formation‑energy mean absolute error from 0.028 eV/atom to 0.024 eV/atom.
Graph networks constitute a universal machine‑learning framework that can accurately predict properties for both molecules and crystals.
Increasing the crystal graph radius cut‑off from 4 Å to 6 Å slightly worsens the formation‑energy mean absolute error (to 0.03 eV/atom), confirming the 4 Å cut‑off as near‑optimal.
CGAT-2 network achieves a mean absolute test error of 21 meV/atom for distance to the convex hull, enabling prediction of thermodynamic stability from unrelaxed crystal structures.
The ML-assisted high-throughput search uncovered 19,512 additional materials on the convex hull of thermodynamic stability after DFT validation.
The ML-assisted high-throughput search spanned approximately 1 billion compounds across 2500 binary and ternary structure prototypes.
Approximately 150,000 compounds were found with energy distance less than 50 meV/atom from the convex hull.
CGAT-2 shows unprecedented generalization accuracy with strongly reduced chemical and structural bias compared to previous models trained on under-represented data.
Compositional models cannot differentiate between polymorphs with the same chemical composition.
The transfer learning approach iterates until model MAE is below 30 meV/atom.
Out of 50 materials screened for electron-phonon calculations, 19 systems were found with Tc above 1 K, with ScMoC2 having the highest transition temperature at 15.97 K.
The ternary compound TiVB3 is predicted to have a superhard hardness of 42 GPa.
Materials within 50 meV/atom from convex hull were selected for subsequent DFT stiffness tensor calculations.

A graph convolutional neural network predicts vibrational free energies with root‑mean‑square errors of 8.23 meV/atom (training), 11.34 meV/atom (validation) and 12.31 meV/atom (test), and its predictions for MgS and NaH polymorphs match DFT‑computed values across the 200–700 K range.

Screening of approximately 50 000 inorganic crystals with the machine‑learning model identified over 2 000 temperature‑induced solid‑solid polymorphic transitions between 300 K and 600 K, including 130 stable transitions within the technologically relevant 300 K–350 K interval.

Twenty‑one stable polar‑nonpolar transitions are predicted to exhibit relative lattice‑thermal‑conductivity changes of at least 20 % (0.20), ranging up to a 73 % increase for ZrSeO with a conductivity ratio of 1.73.

The presented workflow enables high‑throughput prediction of temperature‑induced solid‑solid phase transitions without performing explicit phonon calculations for each material, dramatically reducing computational cost.

Uncertainty quantification based on latent‑space Euclidean distance provides error estimates that correlate with prediction errors, allowing exclusion of transitions whose uncertainty exceeds 50 % of the absolute free‑energy difference.
Metastable phase transitions outnumber stable transitions across all symmetry categories in the screened dataset.
Across the screened temperature range, a larger number of predicted stable phase transitions is generally associated with smaller phase‑transition entropy changes.
The current screening neglects thermal‑expansion effects, which may cause discrepancies with experimental transition temperatures, especially when expansion strongly influences phase stability.

The atomic cluster expansion (ACE) is generalized to model scalar, vectorial and tensorial atomic properties and to include additional atomic degrees of freedom—species, magnetic moments, and charges—on equal footing with atomic positions.
The derived ACE formulas enable efficient evaluation of forces and magnetic torques.
At the lowest order, the magnetic ACE reproduces a distance‑dependent Heisenberg interaction.

Representing tensors with spherical harmonics yields a dramatically sparser basis, where a rank‑N Cartesian tensor with 3^N components can be represented by (N+1)^2 spherical harmonics (e.g., a 10th‑order tensor requires 121 harmonics instead of 59 049 Cartesian components).
Moments Tensor Potentials (MTP) and the Spectral Neighbor Analysis Potential (SNAP) can be expressed exactly as special cases of the ACE.
Because the ACE basis is complete and hierarchical, it can in principle achieve arbitrary accuracy for any scalar, vectorial or tensorial property.

EquiformerV2+DeNS (a universal interatomic potential) achieves the highest classification performance among all evaluated models, with F1 scores up to 0.983, ROC AUC 0.96, and discovery acceleration factors up to 6.33, establishing state‑of‑the‑art for ML‑guided materials discovery.
Random‑forest models excel on small datasets but are outperformed by neural‑network models on large datasets due to the benefits of representation learning.
Models trained on Materials Project data systematically underpredict convex‑hull distances because the training set is biased toward low‑formation‑energy (stable) structures.
High disagreement among model predictions (large standard deviation) can be used to flag potential DFT relaxation failures in high‑throughput screenings.
Accurate regression models can still produce high false‑positive rates near the 0 eV/atom convex‑hull decision boundary.

Using the MACE checkpoint trained on the M3GNet dataset caused volume implosion failures for several hundred of the 250 k test crystals, whereas the checkpoint trained on the MPtrj dataset reduced failures to only 44 crystals.

GNoME achieves hit rates above 80% for structural predictions and 33% for composition-only predictions, compared to 1% in previous work, with active learning improving from less than 6% and 3% respectively over six rounds.
Final GNoME models predict energies with a mean absolute error of 11 meV per atom on relaxed structures, improved from 21 meV per atom in the initial model trained on Materials Project data.

Large-scale pretraining of MLIPs on GNoME dataset enables models with unprecedented zero-shot accuracy on downstream AIMD data, outperforming state-of-the-art NequIP models trained on hundreds of structures from the target distribution.
GNoME discovered crystals correspond to 45,500 novel prototypes, a 5.6x increase from the 8,000 in Materials Project.
GNoME discovers approximately 52,000 layered materials compared to approximately 1,000 in Materials Project, and finds 528 promising Li-ion conductors, a 25x increase compared to the original study.
GNoME enables efficient discovery of materials with 4+ unique elements, which have been difficult for previous discovery efforts.

More than 10⁹ candidate structures were generated over the course of active learning using symmetry-aware partial substitutions and random structure search, with 232,477 out of 381,000 stable structures (approximately 61%) attributed to the SAPS candidate generation procedure.
GNoME-driven molecular dynamics simulations on 623 materials with previously unseen compositions enable classification of unseen compositions as superionic conductors in comparison with AIMD.

Crystal structures, data, and software for analyzing stable crystals, phase diagrams, static GNN, and interatomic potentials will be made available at the Google DeepMind materials_discovery GitHub repository and via the Materials Project with permanent DOI link 10.17188/2009989.
Previous machine-learning techniques have been ineffective in estimating material stability (decomposition energy) with respect to the convex hull.
GNoME discovered 381,000 new stable crystal structures on the convex hull, far exceeding the 13,000 new stable crystals discovered by external research efforts from 2021 to 2023.
91% of 2,202 new Materials Project compositions added since the snapshot match GNoME database on structure.
The GNN predicts atomic von Mises stress in polycrystalline graphene with a mean normalized relative error of 5.5% and a maximum error below 7% on a test set of 400 crystals.
The GNN reproduces the linear decrease of Young’s modulus with vacancy concentration in porous graphene, matching MD results and yielding the fitted relation E = 823.7 − 5635.6·Cv (GPa).

In polycrystalline aluminum, the GNN predicts atomic potential energy with a mean normalized relative error of 11.0% (maximum ≈13%) and achieves R² = 0.99 for mean potential energy versus grain number.
Including tensile strain as an input node feature enables the GNN to accurately predict stress evolution during loading, reproducing nonlinear strain‑stress curves for porous graphene.
The GNN’s stress predictions are substantially more accurate than on‑the‑fly stress calculations from the force field, which exhibit higher errors.

Coupling the GNN with a genetic algorithm efficiently discovers optimal holey graphene designs (e.g., arrow‑shaped hole patterns) that achieve significantly lower stress concentration than suboptimal designs, using only ~800 stress evaluations—an order of magnitude fewer than brute‑force search—and reliably locates the global minimum in most of 1,000 random initializations.

The GNN respects physical constraints, accurately capturing derivative properties such as stress fields that obey underlying physical laws, and predicts global properties (Young’s modulus, total potential energy) that follow known physical relationships and match MD results across different crystalline systems.

The Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation (PNA) GNN model achieves the lowest mean and variance of test mean‑squared error among GCN, GAT, and MPNN (sum and max) variants on the polycrystalline graphene dataset.
The GNN accelerates atomic property prediction by hundreds to thousands of times compared with conventional MD simulations, requiring seconds on a single CPU versus thousands of seconds on 24 CPUs.

Linear fitting of atomic properties yields substantially higher prediction errors than the GNN approach, demonstrating the superiority of the nonlinear GNN model for mapping initial structures to final property distributions.

DeePMD reproduces AIMD energies, forces, and virial tensors for water and ice with root‑mean‑square errors of approximately 1 meV per molecule for energy, 40 meV Å⁻¹ for forces, and 1–2 meV for the virial.
DeePMD accurately reproduces radial distribution functions and three‑body angular distribution functions of liquid water and ice, matching AIMD results.
The computational cost of DeePMD scales linearly with the number of atoms and is several orders of magnitude lower than equivalent AIMD simulations, comparable to empirical force fields.
DeePMD preserves translational, rotational, and permutational symmetries by constructing a local reference frame for each atom and sorting neighbor lists by species and inverse distance.
Using a loss function with adaptive prefactors that emphasize forces early and energies/virial later reduces the total training time to a few core‑hours for all test cases.
Discontinuities in forces caused by the sharp cutoff radius and neighbor‑list sorting are much smaller than thermal fluctuations and do not impair canonical sampling.
DeepH-E3 provides a universal E(3)-equivariant deep-learning framework that exactly preserves Euclidean symmetry of the DFT Hamiltonian, including spin-orbit coupling.

DeepH-E3 predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements with sub‑meV mean absolute error, reducing the error by roughly a factor of two compared with the original DeepH method across diverse material systems.

DeepH-E3 enables accurate electronic‑structure calculations for supercells larger than 10⁴ atoms, reducing computational cost by several orders of magnitude and allowing calculations in minutes on a single GPU versus months on thousands of CPU cores.

DeepH‑E3 reproduces the band structure of magic‑angle twisted bilayer graphene (θ = 1.08°, 11 164 atoms) in excellent agreement with DFT and low‑energy continuum models, correctly capturing the flat bands near the Fermi level.

DeepH‑E3 predicts a spin‑orbit‑coupling‑induced topological quantum phase transition in twisted bilayer Bi₂Te₃, evidenced by band‑gap closing and reopening and a change of the Z₂ invariant from 0 to 1 as SOC strength increases.
DeepH‑E3 attains sub‑meV accuracy after training on only a few hundred DFT calculations of small, non‑twisted structures, demonstrating high data efficiency.
DeepH‑E3 generalizes across diverse material systems—including graphene, MoS₂, bismuthene, Bi₂Se₃, and Bi₂Te₃—achieving consistently sub‑meV Hamiltonian prediction errors.
The model generalizes to arbitrarily twisted bilayer structures; the mean absolute error of Hamiltonian predictions decreases as the Moiré supercell size grows (or twist angle decreases).

The equivariant architecture handles spin‑orbital Hamiltonians by separating real and imaginary components and applying a change‑of‑basis for half‑integer representations, thereby preserving equivariance without requiring complex‑valued network layers.
The model can fit 2.8 × 10⁹ non‑zero complex‑valued Hamiltonian matrix elements with only ~10⁵ real trainable parameters, indicating high capacity efficiency.
EquiformerV2 trained on only OC22 (8.4M structures) achieves better results than GemNet-OC trained on both OC20 (130M structures) and OC22, demonstrating significantly better data efficiency.

EquiformerV2 offers better speed-accuracy trade-offs than Equiformer, being 2.3x faster at Lmax=2 while achieving better force MAE, and requiring 1.4x less training time when increasing Lmax from 2 to 4.

EquiformerV2 incorporates three architectural improvements: attention re-normalization, separable S2 activation, and separable layer normalization, replacing SO(3) convolutions with eSCN convolutions to efficiently incorporate higher-degree tensors.
EquiformerV2 achieves the highest success rate in the AdsorbML algorithm and enables a 2x reduction in DFT calculations needed for computing adsorption energies.
EquiformerV2 achieves better results than Equiformer on 9 out of 12 tasks on the QM9 dataset and is the overall best performing model.
Higher degree representations (larger Lmax) better capture angular resolution and directional information critical for accurate force prediction and correlate with model expressivity.
Attention re-normalization improves energy MAE by 2.4% while force MAE remains approximately the same.

Separable S2 activation prevents large gradients by separating activation for degree 0 and degree > 0 vectors, whereas directly replacing gate activation with S2 activation causes training instability and non-convergence.
MACE uses four-body (higher-order) messages, allowing only two message‑passing layers to achieve converged accuracy, whereas prior equivariant MPNNs required five or six layers.

MACE evaluates roughly ten times faster than prior force‑field models for invariant (L=0) architectures and 4–5 times faster for equivariant (L=1,2) architectures, while delivering lower prediction errors.

MACE shows superior extrapolation ability, reducing energy RMSE by about 30 % at 1200 K and 40 % on dihedral‑slice energies for the 3BPA benchmark, and achieving lower errors on geometries far from the training distribution.
On the 3BPA molecule energy profile, MACE predictions are closest to the DFT ground truth across three dihedral slices, outperforming BOTNet and NequIP.
Increasing the correlation order of messages (ν) steepens the learning‑curve power law, yielding higher data efficiency.
Virtual Node Graph Neural Network (VGNN) enables graph neural networks to handle variable output dimensions by incorporating virtual nodes that resemble phonon dynamical matrices.

Three virtual node approaches were developed: vector virtual nodes (VVN) outputting 3m Γ-phonon branches, matrix virtual nodes (MVN) with m² 3×3 matrices, and momentum-dependent matrix virtual nodes (k-MVN) for full band structure prediction.
VGNN achieves direct prediction of Γ-phonon spectra and full phonon dispersion using only atomic coordinates as input without prior knowledge of interatomic forces.
The approach generalizes to materials with varying atom counts, tested on systems with 2–40 atoms (training) and over 40 atoms (testing).
The model was trained on a DFPT computational database containing phonon dispersion data for 1,521 crystalline inorganic materials.
For very complicated materials, VVN-predicted phonons tend to have higher frequencies than ground truth, and prediction loss becomes larger as input materials become more complicated.
While exact phonon band matching with DFPT is not always achieved, the model captures key features such as average frequency and band gaps.
The Γ-phonon database exhibits a hyperbolic relationship between average frequency and average atomic mass following ω̄ = C m̄^(-1/2) with C ≈ 1993.

The Mixture of Linear Experts (MoLE) architecture enables increasing model capacity without sacrificing inference speed, with a compute-optimal MoLE model achieving equivalent validation loss to dense models using approximately 2.5× fewer active parameters.
UMA sets new state-of-the-art performance on Matbench Discovery and AdsorbML benchmarks, with UMA-M achieving the highest F1 score to date (0.929) on Matbench Discovery.
UMA-M reduces OC20 S2EF adsorption energy prediction errors by approximately 80% compared to previous state-of-the-art models, achieving 33.4 meV MAE versus 149.1 meV for EquiformerV2-OC20.
UMA-S can simulate 1,000 atoms at 16 steps per second (1.4ns per day) and fit system sizes up to 100,000+ atoms in memory on a single 80GB GPU.
A novel two-stage training schedule with BF16 pre-training followed by FP32 fine-tuning recovers the 20-50% accuracy loss from BF16 precision alone while enabling efficient training.
UMA models achieve sub-20 meV/atom energy MAE on multiple molecule benchmarks including biomolecules and electrolytes, and lattice energy prediction accuracy of ≤3 kJ/mol for molecular crystals.
UMA models demonstrate log-linear scaling behavior at compute scales of 10^18-10^20 FLOPs, indicating greater model capacity is required to fit the UMA dataset.
Multi-task UMA models do not overfit to forces during training, unlike single-task models which frequently exhibit force overfitting.
Moving from 1 to 8 experts yields significant loss improvement in MoLE models, while gains from 32 to 128 experts are negligible.
Relaxing test crystals with M3GNet reduces median volume error from 2.4 % to 0.6 % and energy mean absolute error from 0.169 eV/atom to 0.035 eV/atom relative to DFT‑relaxed references.

A single‑CPU M3GNet relaxation completes in about 22 seconds, compared with 15 hours on 32 cores for DFT; pre‑relaxation with M3GNet shortens subsequent DFT relaxation time by roughly a factor of three and reduces total CPU time by an average factor of 2.97.

Screening 31.7 million hypothetical crystals with M3GNet identifies approximately 1.8 million candidates with predicted hull distances below 0.001 eV/atom, and among the 2,000 lowest‑energy candidates, 1,578 are confirmed stable (Ehull < 0.001 eV/atom) by DFT.

M3GNet predicts phonon band structures and densities of states for SiO₂ polymorphs that quantitatively agree with DFT calculations, and the predicted phonon density‑of‑states center follows the expected ω ∝ 1/√m trend across materials.

M3GNet molecular‑dynamics simulations of Li₃YCl₆ reproduce ionic conductivity (14.3 mS cm⁻¹) and activation energy (0.22 eV) consistent with ab‑initio MD, and short‑time MD correctly identifies known lithium superionic conductors by their high mean‑squared displacements at elevated temperatures.

On the MD17 and MD17‑CCSD(T) molecular force‑field benchmarks, M3GNet achieves lower energy and force errors than the Embedded Atom Neural Network and comparable accuracy to state‑of‑the‑art message‑passing and equivariant neural networks; when benchmarked against quantum‑accurate CCSD/CCSD(T) data, it attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for several molecules.

For a MgO test set, M3GNet outperforms Moment Tensor Potentials in extrapolating equation‑of‑state behavior beyond the training regime and exhibits long‑range interaction characteristics similar to a Buckingham + Coulomb model.
The M3GNet architecture preserves continuity of energies, forces, and stresses with respect to changes in bond count, satisfying a necessary physical constraint for interatomic potentials.

The Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD) contains over 200,000 DFT‑calculated crystal structures, including experimental ICSD entries and theoretical prototype structures, and is freely accessible to the scientific community without usage restrictions.
At 0 K and zero pressure, 23 % of the 32,489 ICSD structures in the OQMD are thermodynamically stable according to grand canonical linear programming analysis.
High‑throughput screening identified TiP, LiSiNi₂, and CoSi₂ as the most promising Li‑ion battery anode conversion reactions, offering high capacity, moderate voltage, and low volume expansion.
DFT screening predicts forty‑one previously unreported rare‑earth‑containing Mg‑XL‑XS ternary systems to be thermodynamically stable LPSO phases, providing new experimental targets.

A combined heuristic‑plus‑machine‑learning model trained on OQMD ternary formation energies predicts formation energies with a mean absolute error of ~0.11 eV/atom, roughly half the typical DFT‑experiment error.

Applying the heuristic‑ML model to 1.6 million hypothetical ternary compositions identified nine top candidates, of which eight were confirmed by DFT to be new stable compounds (e.g., SiYb₃F₅, Pa₂O(SiO₆)).
AFLOW can automatically calculate a wide suite of physical observables across a large database of structures with minimal human intervention.

AFLOW detects most calculation failures, automatically corrects input parameters, restarts calculations, and can run as a Unix daemon to generate, run, correct, and converge many DFT jobs per day, yielding higher throughput than manual management.
AFLOW provides a standardized definition of Brillouin‑zone integration paths for all 14 Bravais lattices, filling a gap in the literature.

AFLOW’s cage‑finding algorithm identifies interstitial sites via a topological method, finding 14 cages (6 octahedral, 8 tetrahedral) that reduce to 5 symmetrically inequivalent positions, with radii of 2.2225 Å (octahedral) and 1.9248 Å (tetrahedral).
AFLOW can automatically construct convex hulls for binary alloy systems at zero temperature using formation enthalpies from DFT calculations.
The AFLOW database currently contains approximately 400 experimental prototype structures and several million bcc/fcc/hcp‑derived superstructures.
A hybrid HSE06 calculation for ZnO yields a band gap of 2.48 eV, substantially larger than the LDA/GGA gap of 0.7 eV and the PBE+U gap of 1.82 eV.
Tuning the exact‑exchange fraction α to 0.375 in HSE06 brings the calculated ZnO band gap into agreement with experiment.
AFLOW implements DFT+U using the Dudarev formalism with default Ueff values for a wide range of elements.
A bulk ZnO HSE06 calculation (8×8×6 k‑point mesh, 400 eV cutoff) takes approximately 5 hours on 8 CPUs, while the equivalent GGA/PBE+U calculation finishes in less than a minute.
AFLOW can predict alloy miscibility using Miedema and Hume‑Rothery mixing rules.
The Gaussian approximation potential (GAP) enables atomistic simulations with close-to-DFT accuracy at computational costs many orders of magnitude lower than quantum-mechanical methods.

Combined two-body, three-body, and SOAP many-body descriptors are necessary for GAP to achieve the accuracy limit imposed by force locality and make physically meaningful predictions; models using only subsets of descriptors produce unphysical structures during molecular dynamics simulations.

GAP predicts diamond lattice parameter (3.539 Å) very close to DFT-LDA reference (3.532 Å), outperforming screened Tersoff potential (3.566 Å), with bulk modulus and elastic constants reasonably close to DFT reference values.
GAP radial and angular distribution functions for liquid and amorphous carbon closely match DFT reference results, including peak locations, extents, and overall curve shapes.
GAP recovers three- and four-membered rings that are key features of liquid and low-density amorphous carbon structures, which empirical potentials (Tersoff/Brenner) fail to predict.

Empirical potentials (Tersoff/Brenner) cannot describe interlayer spacing in graphite due to short-range cutoff being less than c/2, provide poor description of carbon surfaces, and yield much lower surface energies than GAP and DFT for ta-C surfaces.
Diamond exhibits strong force locality with force deviations vanishing practically at rfix = 5.5 Å, while graphite is highly nonlocal with larger force deviations that do not decay as rapidly.

For amorphous carbon with 3.7 Å cutoff radius, the lowest achievable standard deviation of force components is approximately 1 eV/Å due to fundamental nonlocality limits, representing a maximum accuracy bound for any finite-range interatomic potential.

DFT-based methods are practically limited to systems of a few hundred atoms, making generation of 8,000-atom amorphous carbon structures impossible with DFT-MD even on state-of-the-art supercomputers.
